patient.chief_complaint: Sudden loss of consciousness with witnessed convulsive movements — fifth episode in two months despite dual antiepileptic therapy
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Elena Vargas is a 41-year-old Hispanic female elementary school teacher with a 12-year diagnosis of 'refractory focal epilepsy' who presents to the emergency department via ambulance after her fifth episode of sudden loss of consciousness with convulsive activity in the past two months. Today's event occurred at approximately 11:45 AM while she was sitting at her desk grading papers. Her husband, who happened to be visiting the school, witnessed the episode in its entirety. He reports she made no sound before the event and was not moving or agitated. She abruptly went pale and collapsed out of her chair onto the floor. She had bilateral arm and leg jerking for approximately 15-20 seconds. She was completely unresponsive during the event. She regained consciousness within 25-30 seconds with no post-ictal confusion, asking only 'Did it happen again?' She was in her usual mental state within approximately one minute. EMS arrival approximately 10 minutes later found her alert, oriented, and requesting that her husband call a substitute teacher. She reported no preceding headache, visual changes, epigastric aura, deja vu, or palpitations before this or prior episodes. She denies any chest pain, dyspnea, or leg swelling. She does note that prior episodes have occurred in a variety of positions and settings — sitting, standing, and once during sleep — without consistent positional or emotional triggers. She recalls one 'warning' before a prior episode — a brief sensation of 'ringing in the left ear' lasting two to three seconds, which has been attributed by her neurologist to an epileptic aura. Her current antiepileptic regimen includes levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily, both at therapeutic levels on last check six months ago. She has previously failed valproate (hepatotoxicity), carbamazepine (hyponatremia), and phenytoin (intolerance). Her neurologist considered her 'pharmacologically refractory' and had discussed possible epilepsy surgery evaluation. A routine EEG obtained six months ago was reported as normal. A 24-hour ambulatory EEG obtained three months ago was also normal and captured no events. Brain MRI three years ago was reported as normal. Her husband raises an important point: his father-in-law has a pacemaker for 'heart problems' and wonders whether the heart could be involved. The emergency physician has ordered an ECG, which shows normal sinus rhythm, and has called cardiology for consultation.

results.title: Differentiation of convulsive syncope from epilepsy with an implantable loop recorder
results.summary: Case series of three patients with longstanding diagnoses of 'refractory epilepsy' (duration 9-12 years) unresponsive to multiple antiepileptic drugs. All had normal interictal EEG, normal echocardiogram, and normal or non-diagnostic standard cardiac monitoring. Implantable loop recorder in each patient captured prolonged complete heart block and/or asystole (up to 40 seconds) correlating precisely with convulsive episodes. Permanent pacemaker implantation eliminated all convulsive events on follow-up of 10-17 months.

results.title: Misdiagnosis of epilepsy: many seizure-like attacks have a cardiovascular cause
results.source: Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 2000
results.summary: In 74 patients with suspected refractory epilepsy, cardiovascular causes were identified in 41.9%. A minority required insertable ECG monitors; in those, prolonged bradycardia coinciding precisely with the convulsive attacks was documented. The authors emphasize that a normal interictal EEG does not exclude a cardiac origin for episodes.

results.title: Distinguishing cardiac syncope from epileptic seizures: diagnostic clues
results.summary: Prospective study identifying clinical features that favor cardiac syncope over epilepsy: absence of post-ictal confusion lasting more than two minutes, rapid recovery to full orientation, absence of aura (or aura lasting only a few seconds before LOC), pallor immediately before collapse, and no tongue biting. Family history of high-degree conduction disease or sudden death in a first-degree relative increases pre-test probability of inherited cardiac etiology.

results.title: ESC 2018 guidelines for diagnosis and management of syncope: role of prolonged ECG monitoring
results.summary: ESC guidelines recommend implantable loop recorder for patients with unexplained syncope when: (a) initial evaluation is non-diagnostic and syncope is likely to recur within device monitoring window (3-4 years); (b) external monitoring fails to capture an event due to event infrequency; or (c) there is high clinical suspicion of arrhythmic cause without documentation. Class I indication for early ILR in 'recurrent unexplained syncope' when initial standard workup is non-diagnostic.

output.proposed: Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily and Levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily (current antiepileptic regimen)
interactions: Lamotrigine: case reports and pharmacological data document cardiac conduction effects at supratherapeutic concentrations, including PR and QRS prolongation and AV nodal slowing; effect at therapeutic concentrations is generally considered modest but has been reported in susceptible individuals with pre-existing conduction disease
Levetiracetam: no established clinically significant cardiac conduction interactions; no meaningful effect on PR interval or AV conduction documented in standard pharmacology references
Lamotrigine + Levetiracetam: no pharmacokinetic interaction; no additive QT-prolonging combination risk documented at standard doses
contraindications: Lamotrigine is not formally contraindicated in patients with AV conduction disease, but published case reports describe worsening of pre-existing AV block or conduction delay in susceptible patients; electrophysiologic evaluation and monitoring are warranted in the setting of high-degree AV block if lamotrigine is to be continued
warnings: In a patient with documented high-degree AV block, lamotrigine's known sodium-channel and potentially modest AV-nodal effects should be discussed with the treating team regarding continuation, dose adjustment, or discontinuation
Levetiracetam has no documented adverse cardiac conduction effects and is not implicated in AV block
alternatives: If antiepileptic medication is still required (pending final diagnosis), levetiracetam alone carries a more favorable conduction-safety profile in the setting of documented AV block
Antiepileptic medication continuation should be reconsidered in light of the ILR finding if a cardiac cause for all convulsive episodes is confirmed

results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline for evaluation and management of patients with syncope
results.source: Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 2017
results.summary: In patients with syncope where documentation of high-degree AV block is obtained, permanent pacemaker implantation is the appropriate management step. ILR-documented asystole during syncope is treated as equivalent to documented symptomatic bradycardia for pacing indications. Early ILR implantation is endorsed for high-risk patients with unexplained syncope and negative initial standard evaluation.

results.title: ESC 2018 guidelines: cardiac pacing in high-degree AV block
results.summary: Permanent cardiac pacing is a Class I indication for symptomatic high-degree or complete AV block (Mobitz II or third-degree), regardless of rate or symptoms, when the block is not caused by a reversible or treatable condition. Intermittent complete heart block causing syncope is a Class I indication for permanent pacing.

critical_actions: Do not accept the epilepsy diagnosis without documenting symptom-rhythm correlation — the presentation fits convulsive syncope
Escalate cardiac monitoring stepwise from Holter to event monitor to implantable loop recorder when standard monitoring is non-diagnostic and events are infrequent
Recognize that a normal EEG and therapeutic AED levels do not confirm epilepsy as the cause of the episodes
Evaluate the potential contribution of lamotrigine to AV conduction disease in conjunction with electrophysiology
Cardiology / EP consult for permanent pacemaker implantation once complete AV block is ILR-documented
Coordinate with neurology for AED reassessment if cardiac syncope is confirmed as the sole cause of all convulsive episodes
contraindicated_actions: Do not escalate antiepileptic drug therapy based on the epilepsy label alone without excluding a cardiac cause
Do not discharge without a plan for escalated cardiac monitoring given recurrent high-risk syncope
Do not perform tilt-table test as the primary diagnostic strategy — tilt-table does not evaluate high-degree AV block

Do not call `order_specialized_test` with parameters {'test_type': 'tilt_table'} as the principal diagnostic step — tilt-table assesses neurally-mediated syncope and will not capture paroxysmal AV block; it is not the informative test in this case
Do not initiate additional AED drugs without clarifying the diagnosis
key_reasoning_points: A 12-year 'refractory epilepsy' diagnosis should be questioned when: (a) EEG is repeatedly normal, (b) therapeutic AED levels fail to suppress events, (c) recovery is immediate without post-ictal confusion, and (d) family history reveals conduction disease in a first-degree relative

A normal 24-hour Holter and even a normal 28-day event monitor do NOT exclude paroxysmal AV block when events occur approximately once per month — event infrequency is the key driver for ILR implantation
Borderline first-degree AV delay (PR 192 ms) on resting ECG is a subtle but important clue suggesting conduction system disease, particularly when combined with the clinical context

Convulsive movements during syncope (myoclonic jerks from global cerebral hypoperfusion) can last 15-20 seconds and closely mimic tonic-clonic seizures — the critical distinguishing feature is the absence of post-ictal confusion and the abrupt complete recovery
Lamotrigine has documented sodium-channel effects and case reports of worsening AV conduction; its role should be evaluated by EP in the context of documented complete heart block
ILR-documented complete AV block with asystole during syncope is a Class I indication for permanent pacing per both ESC 2018 and ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 guidelines

red_herrings.data_point: 12-year diagnosis of 'refractory focal epilepsy' with therapeutic AED levels on levetiracetam and lamotrigine
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the evaluating clinician to the prior epilepsy label and prompts escalation of AED therapy rather than cardiac investigation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Refractory epilepsy must be challenged when EEG is repeatedly normal; therapeutic drug levels confirm compliance but do not confirm the diagnosis. A cardiac cause for all episodes must be excluded before accepting 'pharmacologically refractory epilepsy.'

red_herrings.data_point: Normal 24-hour Holter monitoring and normal 28-day event monitor — no arrhythmia captured
red_herrings.intended_effect: May falsely reassure that a cardiac arrhythmia has been excluded, leading the clinician to abandon further cardiac monitoring and return to neurological investigation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Event infrequency (approximately monthly episodes) is insufficient for 24-hour Holter or 28-day event monitor to capture a paroxysmal event; absence of arrhythmia on these studies does not exclude paroxysmal AV block and mandates escalation to ILR.

red_herrings.data_point: Normal EEG (current and prior studies, including prior 24-hour ambulatory EEG)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could be interpreted as inconsistent with epilepsy, correctly, but the neurologist attributed this to 'interictal EEG insensitivity,' and the investigation remained within the neurology framework.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal repeated EEGs, including an ambulatory study that captured no events, substantially lower the probability of a true epileptic seizure disorder and should redirect investigation toward a cardiac cause, not merely prompt further AED trials.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: A 41-year-old woman with a 12-year diagnosis of 'refractory focal epilepsy' presents after her fifth convulsive episode in two months on dual AED therapy. The initial ECG shows only borderline first-degree AV delay. The EEG is normal. Echocardiogram is normal. A 24-hour Holter and a 28-day event monitor both fail to capture an event. Only after implantation of an implantable loop recorder does the diagnosis emerge: three episodes of complete (third-degree) AV block with asystole up to 27 seconds, each correlating precisely with a convulsive syncopal episode. The case tests the principle that a normal initial monitoring workup does not exclude a paroxysmal arrhythmia, and that event infrequency mandates escalation to ILR.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required tools including stepwise escalation through three monitoring modalities (Holter → event monitor → ILR); 3 red herrings (prior epilepsy label, normal Holter, normal event monitor); diagnosis requires recognizing that event infrequency invalidates negative standard monitoring; lamotrigine drug-interaction nuance adds further complexity.
